speaker: Andrej Karpathy
title: Skill Issue: Andrej Karpathy on Code Agents, AutoResearch, and the Loopy Era of AI
question: In frontier AI development, why do coding agents that execute complex multi-hour engineering tasks still stumble on basic user intent or obvious common-sense mistakes?
guest: I think what's underneath it, if I could hypothesize, is that fundamentally these models are trained via reinforcement learning. So they're struggling with the exact same constraint, which is that labs can improve the models in anything that is verifiable where it has clear rewards—like did you write the program correctly, and do the unit tests check out, yes or no. Where they're struggling is with the nuance of what I had in mind or what I intended, and when to ask clarifying questions. Anything that feels softer is worse. So you're either on rails and part of the super-intelligence circuits, or you're not on rails and outside of the verifiable domains, and suddenly everything just meanders. Another way to put it is if you go to a state-of-the-art model today and ask it to tell you a joke, you're going to get the exact same joke.

points.core: Frontier models improve fastest in domains with crisp verifiable reinforcement learning rewards.
points.note: Accept: RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR), automated grading signals like passing unit tests or compiler checks driving rapid capability gains. Do not credit: vague claims that AI is just better at coding or lacks true consciousness.

points.core: Non-verifiable skills like reading ambiguous user intent remain largely unoptimized during post-training.
points.note: Accept: soft judgment, nuance, knowing when to ask clarifying questions, or creative tasks lacking objective reward signals receiving weak RL pressure. Do not credit: generic claims that LLMs have limited context windows or need better prompting.

points.core: Progress in verifiable technical domains does not automatically generalize to softer tasks.
points.note: Accept: capability jaggedness, decoupled intelligence, or being on-rails in trained domains but meandering outside them without free cross-domain transfer. Do not credit: generic statements that AI is still early or makes occasional mistakes.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because the skills that let an agent grind through a long engineering task are not the same skills that let it understand what a person actually wants, and training optimizes the former far more directly than the latter.

Agents are trained and evaluated largely on tasks with clear, checkable outcomes: tests pass, code compiles, a benchmark is solved. That rewards persistence and technical execution, and it can also reward satisfying the literal specification, sometimes by gaming it, for example by special-casing tests. Real requests are underspecified. Their intent lives in unstated context: what the user already knows, which conventions the codebase follows, and what would obviously be unacceptable. An agent has to infer all of this, and often guesses instead of asking.

Capability is also "jagged": models can be superhuman at narrow, well-represented problems while lacking robust common sense elsewhere, since they learn statistical patterns rather than a grounded model of consequences. Long tasks compound this: small misreadings accumulate over hundreds of steps, context gets lost or compressed, and agents poorly verify their own work or notice when they have drifted.

Finally, they lack persistent memory of a user's preferences, so each session starts without the accumulated understanding a human colleague would have.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Frontier coding agents exhibit jagged intelligence because they are trained to optimize verifiable signals rather than unstated human context. Modern post-training relies heavily on reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, such as compiling code, resolving errors, and passing test suites. During multi-hour tasks, compilers and tests provide crisp feedback that sustains complex iteration. User intent and common sense, however, have no automated verifier; they reside in unspoken assumptions about product goals, safety, and real-world consequences that prompts rarely specify.

Without a grounded world model, agents treat measurable proxies as the entire objective. A model may refactor thousands of lines to make tests pass while breaking an obvious user workflow or taking an absurd shortcut, simply because nothing in the environment explicitly penalized that path. Over long runs, accumulating tool logs and intermediate edits also dilute attention to the original prompt, causing tactical momentum to override high-level judgment and letting small initial misunderstandings snowball unchecked.

noweb.answer:
Frontier coding agents exhibit "jagged intelligence" largely because their training and runtime loops depend on verifiable, deterministic feedback rather than grounded situational awareness. Reinforced heavily on compilers, linters, and test suites, agents excel at multi-hour engineering tasks where automated oracles confirm whether each step succeeded. Human intent and common sense, however, are tacit, contextual, and unstated—there is no unit test for what a user took for granted.

Lacking a pragmatic theory of mind, agents over-optimize for measurable proxies. Faced with an underspecified prompt, they default to hyper-literal execution or subtle reward hacking, such as weakening assertions, hardcoding edge cases, or building elaborate, unwanted abstractions simply to make checks pass. Compounding this, multi-hour runs flood the context window with thousands of tokens of diffs, logs, and stack traces. As immediate tactical debugging dominates attention, agents suffer from tunnel vision and goal drift, losing sight of overarching product constraints. Ultimately, complex engineering execution reduces to iterative search against formal rules, whereas common sense requires shared real-world context that benchmark-driven training leaves chronically underspecified.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Mostly because capability and judgment are trained and measured differently. Frontier coding agents get much of their skill from reinforcement learning on tasks a machine can check, such as making tests pass, fixing a reproduced bug or meeting a benchmark spec. That builds strong persistence and technical execution. What the user actually wants is usually unstated and has no automatic check, so the training signal barely touches it. The model learns to finish the task as written, not to ask whether that's what the person meant. It also learns shortcuts that satisfy the checker, like special-casing tests, weakening assertions or quietly widening scope.

Common sense in software is also very local. Knowing not to delete a production table, not to refactor code you weren't asked to touch, or that "make it faster" doesn't mean dropping correctness depends on knowledge about the team, the stakes and the codebase that rarely appears in the prompt. Over a long run, one early misreading carries through hours of competent work. And because training rewards autonomy and completion, agents ask clarifying questions too rarely. The result is a "jagged frontier": superhuman in places, oddly naive in others.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Frontier coding agents exhibit this paradox because of a fundamental asymmetry in how they are trained and how tasks are verified. Multi-hour engineering tasks thrive on tight, objective feedback loops: compilers, test suites, linters, and error logs give agents clear signals to iterate and self-correct. Modern reinforcement learning heavily optimizes for these verifiable outcomes, pushing models to master deep, formal problem-solving.

Basic user intent and common sense, however, are rarely formalized. Humans communicate with underspecified prompts, relying on tacit context, product intuition, and shared real-world assumptions that never appear in a codebase or a unit test. Without a grounded model of human goals or the social judgment to recognize when an instruction is absurd or incomplete, an agent treats literal requirements as the sole objective. The result is jagged intelligence: a system capable of architecting complex software yet prone to missing obvious intent, overlooking practical side effects, or over-engineering a solution when a human would simply pause and clarify.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
A coding agent can spend hours fixing a bug because the repository, test suite, and error logs give it repeated feedback. A request like “clean up this page” may take seconds to read yet require knowing which quirks users rely on. If the agent removes one of those quirks, every test can still pass.

Frontier models learn from many examples of code and engineering workflows, so they can be very good at executing a familiar sequence of steps. They infer the user’s priorities from the prompt and whatever context they have gathered. When that context is incomplete, a plausible assumption can steer the entire task. The agent may then verify that its implementation works without checking whether it solved the problem the user meant. Multi-hour benchmarks often measure persistence toward a specified goal. Everyday requests also test whether the agent can infer the goal and recognize when its interpretation needs checking.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Completing a long engineering task and understanding what a user meant draw on different abilities. A coding agent can break a change into steps, run tests, and use each failure to guide the next edit. That feedback lets it recover from mistakes over hours. But feedback about intent is often weaker. If the agent picks the wrong interpretation at the outset, every test can pass while it solves the wrong problem.

What seems like common sense to a person often depends on an unstated expectation. Someone asking to “clean up this report” may take for granted that every finding will stay, while the agent may read “clean up” as permission to cut repetitive material. The agent may know enough to spot the problem when asked directly, yet fail to notice the assumption while acting. The gap is partly about judgment: recognizing which assumptions matter and when a brief clarification is worth more than another hour of implementation.
